chunks: "Copper, for almost everything. It has the second-lowest resistivity of any practical metal, about 1.
7 times 10 to the minus 8 ohm-metres, only slightly worse than silver, but it's hundreds of times cheaper.

It's ductile, so it laminates and bends well; it's easy to etch and to electroplate, so you can build up thickness and plate the vias; it solders very well; and it conducts heat well, about 400 watts/mK, so it spreads heat as well as current.
Standard foil is 35 microns, one ounce, with 17. 5 and 70 microns also common. Silver is slightly better electrically but costs far more, tarnishes and has migration problems.
Gold is a worse conductor and extremely expensive, though it's used thinly as a corrosion-proof finish and on contacts.
Aluminium is a worse conductor, forms an oxide that's hard to solder, and plates poorly, so it's used as a heat-sink base in metal-core boards rather than for traces.
The trace sizing follows from copper's properties: roughly a 10 mil, 0. 25 mm, trace of 1 ounce copper carries about 0.
9 amps for a 10 degree rise, and I'd go to 2 ounce or wider traces for power. And remember copper's resistance rises about 0. 4% per degree, so hot traces are more resistive."
